old: prasūyate can also be taken as active 'produces' (lamp as subject); passive with kajjalam as subject is preferred. In the second line the subject of bhakṣayate is not expressed ('one'); Hindi uses the passive for this. 'yat annam' has no 'tat' in the Sanskrit.
new: prasūyate is read as passive/middle 'is produced' with kajjalam as subject. In the second line the subject of bhakṣayate is not expressed ('one'); Hindi uses the passive for this. 'yat annam' has no 'tat' in the Sanskrit.
why: reviewer (minor): Claim that prasūyate could be active 'produces' is not sound: sūyate is passive/middle, active sense would be sūte.

old: Four printed lines form one verse (two halves of a longer metre, 19 syllables each); the first two lines are the statement and the last two a comparison. 'gacchantam' is a masculine accusative form, while 'tat' (neuter) would take 'gacchat'; it is read as 'that (water) going to the ocean', and the metre supports the printed form. 'na ... kvacit' is read as 'not anywhere'. 'tat' is taken to refer to the jalam of line b; the text does not say 'water' in line d.
new: Four printed lines form one verse (four pādas of 19 syllables each, scanning as śārdūlavikrīḍita); the first two lines are the statement and the last two a comparison. 'gacchantam' is a masculine accusative form, while 'tat' (neuter) would take 'gacchat'; it is read as 'that (water) going to the ocean', and the metre supports the printed form. 'na ... kvacit' is read as 'not anywhere'. 'tat' is taken to refer to the jalam of line b; the text does not say 'water' in line d.
why: reviewer (error): 'two halves of a longer metre' is wrong. Each of the four pādas scans as 19 syllables in śārdūlavikrīḍita (ma sa ja sa ta ta ga), so the four printed lines are four pādas of one verse.

old: The subject 'he' is not expressed. 'ca' after 'na' joins the clause to the list of occasions and is left untranslated as it adds no separate sense. 'citādhūme' read as 'smoke of the funeral pyre'.

old: In indigestion water is medicine, once digested water gives strength; and in a meal water is nectar, at the end of the meal it removes poison.
new: In indigestion water is medicine, when digested water gives strength; and in a meal water is nectar, at the end of the meal it removes poison.
why: reviewer (minor): 'once' is not in the Sanskrit; parallel ajīrṇe is simply locative. Use 'when digested' (Hindi already 'पच जाने पर').
